So are Jensen Huang’s problems.

   The reinstatement of Nvidia’s chief executive Monday reinvigorated the company’s stock and gave new life to the AI trade. But the move also raises tricky questions about the company’s role as an underwriter of the AI boom and how it manages Huang’s exposure to national-security scrutiny.

   Nvidia’s importance to the markets has been clearly demonstrated. So have the risks if it falters again. And the ingredients for a potential stumble are already there in Nvidia’s financial support for companies that buy its chips.

   Below, some of the best analysis and insight from WSJ writers and columnists, the Dow Jones Newswires team and occasionally beyond, on investing, the wealth-management business and more.

       Planning & Investing   The Retail Investors Who Believed Nvidia’s Board—and Got Burned by Its U-Turn   Nvidia’s board said as recently as last week that Jensen Huang wouldn’t return as CEO. Some investors sold their shares.

       Market Talk   From Dow Jones Newswires 

   Europe’s diversified financial stocks should benefit from another year of double-digit growth in earnings per share, Barclays analysts write. The sector contains a range of businesses that have a supportive market backdrop, even if the interest-rate outlook is uncertain, Barclays says. Strong cost control can also drive margin expansion in the sector, the analysts add. The subsector fell the most in the financials sector in 2026, driven by the performance of alternative asset managers. As a result, the sector’s valuation looks attractive, Barclays says, with shares trading at a 9% discount to long-term multiples. Strong cash generation offers multiple options for diversified financial companies, including dividends, buybacks and mergers and acquisitions, the analysts note. (Michael Hennessey, michael.hennessey@wsj.com)

   French President Emmanuel Macron’s proposal to help stabilize the country’s fiscal outlook is unlikely to fix its problems, Charlotte de Montpellier at ING says in a note. The so-called “golden rule” would create multiyear framework laws, adding legal spending restraints to annual budgets. But the rule would fall short of setting a debt target, and a subsequent organic law would be needed to determine how compliance would be assessed. Furthermore, parliament could potentially make modifications, while approving the rule may not gain enough political support. “France’s central problem…is less the absence of rules than the absence of political willingness to implement them.” More important will be passing a credible budget, though this is easier said than done, de Montpellier says. (Don Forbes, don.forbes@wsj.com)

Nvidia’s Role as an Underwriter of the AI Boom
 
Plus, the hidden price of remote work and the Thanksgiving parade’s new star
 
 
PHILIP FONG/AGENCE FRANCE-PRESSE/GETTY IMAGES
 

Jensen Huang is back. So are Jensen Huang’s problems.

 

The reinstatement of Nvidia’s chief executive Monday reinvigorated the company’s stock and gave new life to the AI trade. But the move also raises tricky questions about the company’s role as an underwriter of the AI boom and how it manages Huang’s exposure to national-security scrutiny.

 

Nvidia’s importance to the markets has been clearly demonstrated. So have the risks if it falters again. And the ingredients for a potential stumble are already there in Nvidia’s financial support for companies that buy its chips.

 

Below, some of the best analysis and insight from WSJ writers and columnists, the Dow Jones Newswires team and occasionally beyond, on investing, the wealth-management business and more.

Nvidia’s board said as recently as last week that Jensen Huang wouldn’t return as CEO. Some investors sold their shares.

 
 
 

Market Talk

 

From Dow Jones Newswires

 

Europe’s diversified financial stocks should benefit from another year of double-digit growth in earnings per share, Barclays analysts write. The sector contains a range of businesses that have a supportive market backdrop, even if the interest-rate outlook is uncertain, Barclays says. Strong cost control can also drive margin expansion in the sector, the analysts add. The subsector fell the most in the financials sector in 2026, driven by the performance of alternative asset managers. As a result, the sector’s valuation looks attractive, Barclays says, with shares trading at a 9% discount to long-term multiples. Strong cash generation offers multiple options for diversified financial companies, including dividends, buybacks and mergers and acquisitions, the analysts note. (Michael Hennessey, michael.hennessey@wsj.com)

 

French President Emmanuel Macron’s proposal to help stabilize the country’s fiscal outlook is unlikely to fix its problems, Charlotte de Montpellier at ING says in a note. The so-called “golden rule” would create multiyear framework laws, adding legal spending restraints to annual budgets. But the rule would fall short of setting a debt target, and a subsequent organic law would be needed to determine how compliance would be assessed. Furthermore, parliament could potentially make modifications, while approving the rule may not gain enough political support. “France’s central problem…is less the absence of rules than the absence of political willingness to implement them.” More important will be passing a credible budget, though this is easier said than done, de Montpellier says. (Don Forbes, don.forbes@wsj.com)
